etching-001.question: Which correctly describes anisotropic etching?
choices: Etching proceeds mainly vertically and hardly at all laterally
Etching proceeds at the same rate in all directions
Only the mask material is selectively removed
etching-001.explanation: In anisotropic etching, vertically accelerated ion bombardment and sidewall-protecting passivation make etching proceed preferentially downward, with almost no lateral undercut beneath the mask. Mask patterns are thus transferred without dimensional change, enabling fine vertical features such as tens of nm wide and several µm deep. Etching that proceeds equally in all directions is isotropic.

etching-002.question: Which correctly describes 'selectivity' in etching?
choices: The ratio of film thickness before and after etching
The ratio of etch rates at the center and edge of the wafer
The ratio of the etch rate of the target film to that of the mask or underlying film
etching-002.explanation: Selectivity is the ratio of the etch rate of the film being removed to that of a film that should remain (mask or underlying layer). Gate etching, for example, may need selectivity above 100 to the underlying gate dielectric only a few nm thick. Higher selectivity permits thinner masks and spares underlying layers. Variation of etch rate across the wafer is called uniformity.

etching-003.question: Which is a general characteristic of wet etching?
choices: It is highly anisotropic because it uses plasma
It generally proceeds isotropically and readily undercuts the mask
etching-003.explanation: Wet etching dissolves films by chemical reaction in liquid, so it generally proceeds equally in all directions (isotropic) and undercuts the mask by about the film thickness. It needs simple equipment, processes many wafers at once and easily achieves high selectivity. Dry etching is used for fine patterning, but wet etching remains important for blanket film removal and cleaning.

etching-004.question: Which correctly describes reactive ion etching (RIE)?
choices: Etching that combines chemical reactions and ion bombardment in a plasma of reactive gases
Etching by immersing the wafer in a chemical solution
Grinding the wafer surface with a polishing pad
etching-004.explanation: Reactive ion etching (RIE) combines chemical reactions driven by radicals from a reactive-gas plasma (fluorine- or chlorine-based, etc.) with bombardment by ions accelerated in an electric field. Ions striking perpendicular to the wafer promote reactions at the feature bottom, so etching proceeds vertically with high anisotropy. Despite the name, ions do not etch alone; the synergy with radicals is the essence.

etching-005.question: Which method is commonly used to detect the endpoint of dry etching?
choices: Monitoring changes in the plasma's emission spectrum
etching-005.explanation: When the film being etched clears and the underlayer is exposed, the species and amounts of reaction products in the plasma change, altering emission intensity at specific wavelengths—for oxide etching, CO emission at 483 nm drops. Monitoring this with optical emission spectroscopy (OES) detects the endpoint in real time. When the exposed area is very small the signal is weak, so interferometric thickness monitoring is also used.

etching-006.question: What is the aspect ratio of a hole or trench formed by etching?
choices: The ratio of depth to width (opening diameter)
The ratio of top area to bottom area
The ratio of the etch rates of the target film and the mask
etching-006.explanation: Aspect ratio is a feature's depth divided by its width—a hole 100 nm across and 1 µm deep has an aspect ratio of 10. 3D NAND memory holes about 100 nm wide reach several µm deep, giving aspect ratios of 50–100. In such deep, narrow features, ions and radicals struggle to reach the bottom and profiles distort easily, making them a central challenge in etching. A ratio of etch rates is selectivity.

etching-007.question: What is the phenomenon called in which the etch rate decreases as patterns become narrower and deeper?
etching-007.explanation: At the bottom of narrow, deep features, radicals are lost to wall collisions, ions are deflected by charging, and reaction products escape slowly, so etch rate falls as aspect ratio rises. This aspect-ratio-dependent etching (ARDE, or microloading) leaves narrow holes shallower than wide ones on the same wafer, so depths vary with size. Etch-stop layers and process tuning compensate.

etching-008.question: Which gases are commonly used for dry etching of polysilicon gates?
choices: Halogen gases such as chlorine (Cl2) and hydrogen bromide (HBr)
etching-008.explanation: Polysilicon is commonly etched with halogen gases such as chlorine and hydrogen bromide. They react with silicon to form volatile SiCl4 and SiBr4 while barely attacking oxide, giving selectivity above 100 to the thin underlying gate oxide. HBr also readily forms sidewall passivation for vertical profiles, and small oxygen additions tune the amount of passivation.

etching-009.question: What is the process called that removes photoresist by oxidizing it to ash with oxygen plasma or similar?
etching-009.explanation: Ashing oxidizes resist organics in an oxygen plasma or similar, removing them as CO2 and H2O—hence the name, from turning the resist to ash. It strips resist after it has served as an etch or implant mask, followed by wet cleaning to remove residue. Downstream (radical-only) ashers are common to avoid damage, and hydrogen-based plasmas replace oxygen over low-k films.

etching-010.question: Which is a characteristic of atomic layer etching (ALE)?
choices: It etches several µm quickly in one step
It alternates surface modification and removal, controlling the etched amount at the atomic-layer level
It is isotropic wet etching using chemical solutions
etching-010.explanation: ALE repeats self-limiting steps: first modify only the top surface layer, e.g., by chlorine adsorption, then remove just that layer with low-energy ions or similar. With a fixed removal of about 0.1–0.5 nm per cycle, it offers atomic-scale control, low surface damage and little dependence on pattern density. The etching counterpart of ALD, it is entering use in GAA and gate-region processing.

etching-011.question: Which correctly describes one mechanism by which dry etching achieves anisotropy?
choices: A passivation film deposited on the sidewalls prevents lateral etching, while ion bombardment removes it from the bottom so etching proceeds there
The chemical solution reacts equally in all directions
etching-011.explanation: In dry etching, polymer derived from gases such as fluorocarbons and from reaction products deposits on sidewalls and blocks lateral etching, while ions striking the bottom vertically clear the film so etching proceeds downward. Too much passivation tapers the profile; too little causes bowing, so gas chemistry and temperature are balanced to achieve vertical sidewalls.

etching-012.question: Which solution is commonly used for wet etching of silicon nitride?
etching-012.explanation: Silicon nitride is etched in concentrated phosphoric acid heated to about 160 °C with selectivity of tens to over 100 to oxide. It removes nitride masks after LOCOS or STI formation and, in 3D NAND, strips the nitride layers from alternating oxide/nitride stacks so they can be replaced with word-line metal. Selectivity depends on dissolved silicon in the bath, requiring tight control.

etching-013.question: During plasma etching, what is the phenomenon called in which conductors acting as antennas, such as long wires, collect charge and damage the gate oxide they connect to?
etching-013.explanation: Conductors exposed to plasma collect charge, and when it flows as tunneling current through the thin oxide of a connected gate, the oxide degrades or breaks down. Larger conductor area (the antenna) collects more charge, so layouts follow antenna rules limiting the ratio of conductor area to gate area; violations are fixed with protection diodes that bleed off charge or by changing metal layers.

etching-014.question: Which is a characteristic of wet etching of silicon with potassium hydroxide (KOH) solution?
choices: Etch rates differ greatly between crystal planes, and the (111) plane etches very slowly, producing features such as V-shaped grooves with sloped walls
It is isotropic etching that proceeds at the same rate on all crystal planes
etching-014.explanation: Alkaline solutions such as KOH etch silicon's (111) planes about 100 times slower than (100) planes, so on (100) wafers the (111) planes emerge, forming V-grooves and pyramidal pits with sidewalls at about 54.7°. This crystallographic anisotropy is used to make MEMS pressure-sensor diaphragms, inkjet nozzles and light-trapping surface textures on solar cells.

etching-015.question: Which is a characteristic of inductively coupled plasma (ICP) etching equipment?
choices: It generates high-density plasma with a coil, and plasma density and ion energy are easy to control separately
etching-015.explanation: An ICP etcher drives RF current through a coil above or around the chamber to induce an electric field that sustains a dense plasma of 10¹¹–10¹² cm⁻³, while a separate RF supply biases the wafer. Plasma density (radical and ion flux) and ion energy at the wafer can be set independently, enabling fast, highly anisotropic etching at pressures of a few Pa or less; ICP tools are widely used for silicon and metal etching.

etching-016.question: Which metric indicates how small the variation in etch rate is across the wafer?
etching-016.explanation: Uniformity describes how consistent etch rate and profile are across the wafer, for example expressed as (max − min) ÷ (2 × mean) in percent. Poor uniformity leaves residue in some places and overetches others, cutting yield at the wafer edge. Plasma density distribution, gas flow, multi-zone wafer temperature control and focus rings are tuned to bring it below a few percent.

etching-017.question: After the etch endpoint is detected, what is it called to continue etching for a set time to ensure the film is removed across the whole wafer?
etching-017.explanation: Because of etch-rate and thickness variation across the wafer and film remaining on step sidewalls, some film may remain when the endpoint is detected. An overetch—often about 20–50% of the main etch time—ensures complete removal. Since exposed underlayers keep etching during this step, conditions are usually switched to ones with high selectivity to the underlayer.

etching-018.question: What is a mask of nitride, carbon or similar material called, used when photoresist alone cannot survive as a mask, such as when etching deep holes?
etching-018.explanation: Deep etches would consume resist only about 100 nm thick before finishing, so the resist pattern is first transferred into a nitride, oxide or amorphous-carbon layer, which then masks the main etch—a hard mask. For 3D NAND's deep holes, amorphous-carbon hard masks several µm thick are used, making their deposition and removal important steps in their own right.

etching-019.question: Which is a characteristic of downstream etching, which supplies only plasma-generated radicals to the wafer?
choices: Strong ion bombardment makes it highly anisotropic
With almost no ion bombardment, it etches isotropically with little damage
etching-019.explanation: In downstream (remote-plasma) etching, the plasma is generated away from the wafer, and ions and electrons recombine en route, so only long-lived neutral radicals reach it. With no ion bombardment and plasma UV blocked, damage is minimal and etching is isotropic. It is used for resist stripping, damage-sensitive film removal and selectively removing SiGe between nanosheets.

etching-020.question: Which are examples of profile defects seen in high-aspect-ratio etching?
choices: Bowing, where the hole widens partway down, and twisting, where the hole bends
Dishing, where wiring becomes dish-shaped in CMP
Shadowing, where tilted implants create shadows
etching-020.explanation: Deep-hole etching is prone to profile defects: bowing, where ions scattered from mask edges widen the hole partway down; twisting, where charging at the bottom deflects ions so holes bend or spiral; and tapering that fails to open the bottom. In 3D NAND, keeping memory holes straight with uniform diameter through hundreds of layers is a major challenge, addressed with cryogenic etching and other techniques.

etching-021.question: If the oxide etch rate is 100 nm/min and the mask is consumed at 20 nm/min, what is the selectivity to the mask?
etching-021.explanation: Selectivity is the etch rate of the target film divided by that of the mask (or underlayer): 100 ÷ 20 = 5. Etching 500 nm of oxide consumes 100 nm of mask, so allowing for overetch and edge erosion the mask should be at least about 150–200 nm thick. If selectivity is insufficient, a thicker mask or a hard mask is used.

etching-022.question: Which solution, made by buffering hydrofluoric acid with ammonium fluoride, is used for wet etching of SiO2?
etching-022.explanation: Buffered hydrofluoric acid (BHF) adds ammonium fluoride to HF to stabilize pH, so the concentration of the main etching species (HF2⁻) changes little as the bath is consumed, keeping etch rates steady and resist intact. It etches thermal oxide at tens to about 100 nm per minute and has been used for oxide patterning, native-oxide removal and film-quality evaluation.

etching-023.question: Why is cryogenic etching, which cools the wafer to very low temperatures, attracting attention for high-aspect-ratio processing?
choices: Because the etch rate becomes zero
Because reactions on the sidewalls are suppressed, making fast, vertical deep etching easier
Because plasma is no longer needed
etching-023.explanation: Cooling the wafer to cryogenic temperatures (e.g., below −60 °C) suppresses spontaneous radical reactions on sidewalls, where condensed gases and products act as passivation, while ion-bombarded bottoms keep etching. Deep, vertical holes can reportedly be etched more than twice as fast as conventionally, so cryogenic etching is being adopted for 3D NAND memory holes. Chamber cooling technology and gas choices such as hydrogen fluoride are key.

etching-024.question: Because changes in the condition of an etch chamber's walls alter results, what is it called to process dummy wafers before product to stabilize the chamber?
etching-024.explanation: Reaction products coat etch-chamber walls, and their condition changes how many radicals are lost at the walls, shifting plasma chemistry and results. Seasoning runs dummy wafers after cleaning or part replacement to build a consistent wall coating and stabilize performance. Some processes now reset the walls to the same state before every wafer.

etching-025.question: What is an advantage of pulsed plasma, which etches while switching the RF power on and off?
choices: Electron temperature and ion energy are easier to control, making charging and damage easier to suppress
etching-025.explanation: In pulsed plasmas, electron temperature drops sharply during off-periods of tens of µs and negative ions form, helping neutralize wafer charging. Duty cycle and pulse frequency also tune ion energy and the mix of radical species, so pulsing is used at advanced nodes to suppress notching and electron-shading profile defects and to limit damage to gate dielectrics.

etching-026.question: Which gases are commonly used for dry etching of GaN?
etching-026.explanation: GaN's strong bonds make it chemically stable and nearly immune to wet etching, but chlorine-based plasmas remove it as volatile GaCl3, with BCl3 also helping strip surface oxide. High-density ICP tools etch mesas for LEDs and lasers and gate recesses for HEMTs, using low ion energies to keep etch damage from degrading performance.

etching-027.question: Why is it difficult to pattern copper wiring directly by dry etching?
choices: Because copper does not conduct electricity
Because copper halides are not volatile, so the reaction products cannot be removed
etching-027.explanation: Aluminum reacts with chlorine to form volatile aluminum chloride and can be dry-etched, but copper chlorides do not volatilize below several hundred °C and remain on the surface. Copper wiring is therefore made without etching the metal: trenches in the dielectric are filled with copper and the excess removed by CMP (damascene). For very fine wires, etchable metals such as ruthenium are being explored.

etching-028.question: In gate etching, what is the phenomenon called in which the pattern sidewall is undercut laterally near the boundary with the underlying insulator?
etching-028.explanation: Notching occurs after etching reaches the underlying dielectric: positive ion charge accumulates on the insulator, deflecting incoming ions sideways so the base of the pattern is undercut. It is worst at the edges of patterns and locally changes gate length, causing transistor variation. Remedies include pulsed plasma or low-frequency bias to reduce charging and tuned overetch conditions.

etching-029.question: Why are reaction products (polymers) left on pattern sidewalls removed after dry etching?
choices: To prevent defects in later steps and degradation of electrical characteristics
To change the color of the wafer
etching-029.explanation: Polymer left on sidewalls from etching can weaken adhesion of subsequent films, raise contact resistance and—when chlorine-bearing residue remains—corrode aluminum wiring. It is carefully removed by ashing and cleaning with organic or fluoride-based chemistries. At advanced nodes, cleans must be strong enough to remove residue yet gentle enough not to damage low-k dielectrics or thin metals.

etching-030.question: What is needed to etch oxide and stop on the nitride underneath?
choices: High etch selectivity of oxide to nitride
etching-030.explanation: Stopping on nitride requires conditions that etch oxide quickly while barely touching nitride. Carbon-rich fluorocarbons such as C4F6 or C4F8 deposit polymer on nitride that halts the reaction, whereas oxygen released from oxide consumes the polymer so oxide keeps etching, yielding selectivity of several tens or more. This is crucial for forming self-aligned contacts.

etching-031.question: What is the role of etching in semiconductor manufacturing?
choices: Removing film from areas not covered by a mask such as resist to form patterns
etching-031.explanation: Etching removes film or substrate not protected by a mask—typically the resist pattern from lithography—by chemical reaction and ion bombardment, sculpting circuit patterns. It must transfer resist dimensions faithfully into the film below, holding dimensional changes to about 1 nm or less at advanced nodes. Paired with lithography, it is repeated dozens of times in IC fabrication.
choiceNotes: Correct. Uncovered areas are removed to form patterns.
Diffusing impurities is a heat-treatment step.
Adding films is the deposition step.

etching-032.question: Which correctly describes the "plasma" used in dry etching?
choices: A state of gas that is ionized, containing a mixture of electrons, ions, radicals and so on
etching-032.explanation: A plasma is a gas energized—by RF power, for example—so accelerated electrons ionize atoms and molecules, producing a mixture of electrons, ions, highly reactive radicals and neutral molecules; it is often called the fourth state of matter. Etch-tool plasmas are weakly ionized (below 1%, often 0.01% or less in capacitively coupled tools) "low-temperature plasmas," in which the gas stays cool while electrons carry energies equivalent to tens of thousands of degrees.
choiceNotes: Plasma is not a liquid.
Correct. It is an ionized state of gas.
Plasma is not a solid.

etching-033.question: If etching proceeds at 100 nm/min for 3 minutes, how much film is removed?
etching-033.explanation: Material removed equals etch rate × time: 100 nm/min × 3 min = 300 nm. In practice, variations in thickness and rate mean a short overetch follows endpoint detection. Working backward, a 500 nm film needs 5 minutes, or about 6 minutes with 20% overetch. Tools manage this by combining timed steps with endpoint detection.
choiceNotes: About 3,000 nm is an order of magnitude too large.
About 33 nm is 100 divided by 3.
Correct. 100 × 3 = 300 nm.

etching-034.question: In wet etching, how does the etch rate generally change when the solution temperature is raised?
etching-034.explanation: Wet etching proceeds by chemical reaction, so higher temperature generally speeds it up—often by 1.5–2× per 10 °C. Stable removal therefore requires bath temperature control to about ±0.5 °C. Some chemistries, such as hot phosphoric acid for nitride (about 160 °C), are intentionally used at high temperature.
choiceNotes: The etch rate depends strongly on temperature.
Correct. The reaction speeds up and the etch rate rises.
Raising the temperature generally speeds up reactions.

etching-035.question: In plasma tools such as capacitively coupled ones, what is the phenomenon called in which the wafer-side electrode naturally acquires a negative DC potential that accelerates ions toward the wafer?
etching-035.explanation: On an RF-driven electrode, light, mobile electrons flow in more readily than ions, so a capacitively coupled electrode settles at a negative average DC potential—the self-bias, tens to hundreds of volts. This potential accelerates positive ions from the plasma nearly vertically into the wafer, enabling anisotropic etching. Changing RF power changes the self-bias and thus ion energy.
choiceNotes: The Hall effect is a voltage perpendicular to current in a magnetic field.
The Seebeck effect is a voltage produced by a temperature difference.
Correct. A negative potential arises from the difference in electron flow.

etching-036.question: What is the masking scheme called that stacks three layers, an organic (carbon) film at the bottom, a silicon-containing middle layer and resist on top, to etch fine patterns deeply?
etching-036.explanation: In a trilayer stack, the thin resist pattern is first transferred into a silicon-containing middle layer (such as SiARC) with fluorine plasma, which then masks a thick organic underlayer (spin-on carbon) etched in oxygen plasma. Silicon-bearing films resist oxygen plasma and organics resist fluorine chemistry, so chaining these high selectivities turns a thin resist into a thick, robust mask. The middle layer also serves as an anti-reflective coating.
choiceNotes: Correct. Three layers are stacked and the pattern is transferred in sequence.
Damascene forms wiring by filling trenches with metal.
LOCOS is isolation by selective oxidation.

etching-037.question: Which gas can etch silicon isotropically without a plasma, for example to remove sacrificial layers in MEMS?
etching-037.explanation: XeF2 sublimes near room temperature and reacts spontaneously with silicon to form SiF4 (2XeF2 + Si → 2Xe + SiF4), etching silicon isotropically without plasma. Its selectivity to oxide, nitride, resist and many metals exceeds 1000, and because no liquid is involved stiction is avoided, so it is used to release MEMS structures from silicon sacrificial layers.
choiceNotes: Oxygen is used to remove organic materials such as resist.
Nitrogen does not etch silicon.
Correct. It is a gas that etches silicon without plasma.

etching-038.question: Which technique gradually thins an exposed resist pattern with plasma to create lines narrower than the exposure limit?
etching-038.explanation: Resist trimming isotropically erodes resist lines a little at a time with oxygen-based plasma to narrow them—printing 50 nm lines and trimming them to 30 nm, for example. It has been used to form gates narrower than lithography can resolve. It does not shrink pitch, however, and variations in trim amount and LER translate directly into dimensional variation, so control is critical.
choiceNotes: Correct. It thins the resist to make narrow lines.
Reflow heats a film to make it flow.
Edge bead removal clears resist from the wafer edge.

etching-039.question: In gate electrode etching, what is commonly done to preserve the thin gate insulator underneath?
choices: Etching with the same aggressive conditions from start to finish
Etching most of the way with fast conditions, then switching to conditions with high selectivity to the underlayer as it is approached
Continuing with aggressive conditions for a while after the underlayer appears
etching-039.explanation: Gate etching first removes most of the material with a fast main-etch step that sets the profile, then, after endpoint, switches to a high-selectivity overetch that clears residual film at steps while barely touching the few-nm dielectric below. Splitting the etch into stages achieves both vertical profiles and underlayer protection. Punching through the gate dielectric would gouge the silicon and ruin the transistor.
choiceNotes: Aggressive conditions throughout would also etch the thin underlayer.
Correct. Conditions are switched in stages to preserve the underlayer.
Continuing aggressive etching would punch through the underlayer.

etching-040.question: When a 1 µm film is etched just down to the underlayer by perfectly isotropic wet etching, roughly how much is etched laterally from the mask edge (undercut)?
etching-040.explanation: Isotropic etching proceeds equally downward and sideways, so by the time 1 µm of film clears to the underlayer, the mask edge is undercut by about 1 µm, and overetch increases this further. Dimensional changes on the order of the film thickness make it unsuitable for features narrower than the film is thick. Conversely, MEMS exploits this behavior to hollow out material beneath structures.
choiceNotes: Correct. About 1 µm is etched laterally, the same as vertically.
In isotropic etching, the lateral amount is about the same as the vertical, not ten times.
No lateral etching is the case for ideal anisotropic etching.

etching-041.question: Which metric expresses how far the sidewall of an etched hole or trench tilts from vertical?
etching-041.explanation: Taper angle describes sidewall slope, with angles near 90° indicating highly anisotropic etching; heavy passivation produces tapered profiles with smaller angles. Features that will later be filled may benefit from a slight taper (around 85°) for void-free filling, whereas gates and fins are made nearly vertical to minimize top-to-bottom dimension differences, so taper is controlled per application.
choiceNotes: Aspect ratio is the ratio of depth to width.
Correct. It is the angle of the sidewall slope.
Selectivity is the ratio of etch rates, such as film to mask.

etching-042.question: What is the general effect of adding a little oxygen to fluorine-based etching gas?
choices: Selectivity to the mask always increases
Polymer deposition on sidewalls and elsewhere decreases, and the resist erodes faster
etching-042.explanation: Oxygen burns off carbon-containing polymer as CO and CO2, reducing deposition on sidewalls and surfaces, and by scavenging carbon from fluorocarbons it frees more fluorine radicals, speeding etching. Resist is also eroded more readily by oxygen, so mask selectivity tends to fall. Additions are tuned in percent-level steps to balance profile against selectivity.
choiceNotes: A small amount of oxygen does not stop etching.
Because resist erodes more easily, selectivity actually tends to drop.
Correct. Polymer decreases and the resist erodes faster.

etching-043.question: In a typical etching plasma, how do the numbers of ions and radicals compare?
etching-043.explanation: In a plasma, dissociation into radicals requires less energy than ionization and occurs more readily, and radicals, being uncharged, are not drawn to the walls and live longer. Radical densities therefore typically exceed ion densities by two to three orders of magnitude or more. Radicals carry out most of the chemistry, while the scarcer ions promote reactions through bombardment and set the etch direction.
choiceNotes: They differ in how easily they form and how long they live, so their numbers differ.
Correct. Radicals typically outnumber ions by orders of magnitude.
Under typical conditions, ions are fewer.

etching-044.question: Which method inserts a small electrode into a plasma and measures the current as the voltage is varied to determine the plasma's electron temperature and density?
etching-044.explanation: A Langmuir probe inserts a small electrode into the plasma and measures current while sweeping the applied voltage. The curvature of the I-V characteristic gives electron temperature (a few eV), saturation currents give electron and ion densities, and the knee gives the plasma potential. Devised by Langmuir in the 1920s, it is the most basic plasma diagnostic, though the probe can perturb the plasma and become coated with deposits.
choiceNotes: The four-point probe measures film or wafer resistivity.
X-ray diffraction examines crystal structure.
Correct. The plasma is evaluated from the probe's I-V characteristic.

etching-045.question: In dry etching, what is the profile defect called in which the bottom of a trench is etched deeper near the sidewalls than in the center, creating narrow grooves?
etching-045.explanation: Microtrenching is localized deeper etching at the bottom corners of trenches and holes. It is attributed to ions reflecting off sloped sidewalls and concentrating at the corners, and to ions deflected by sidewall charging. In gate and STI etching it can punch through underlayers at the corners or create filling and field-concentration problems later, so pressure, bias and gas chemistry are tuned to suppress it.
choiceNotes: Correct. The bottom corners are etched locally deeper.
Bowing is a barrel-like lateral bulge partway down the sidewall.
Mask recession is mask erosion that changes dimensions.

etching-046.question: Exposing silicon to XeF2 gas and an argon ion beam simultaneously etches it far faster than the sum of either alone. What property of dry etching does this show?
choices: Ions play no role in etching
The synergy between ions and radicals (ion assistance)
etching-046.explanation: In Coburn and Winters' 1979 experiment, XeF2 alone or argon ions alone etched silicon slowly, but together they etched about ten times faster than the sum. Ion bombardment creates a disordered, more reactive surface layer and helps desorb reaction products. This synergy (ion-assisted etching) makes ion-struck feature bottoms etch rapidly, giving RIE its fast, anisotropic character.
choiceNotes: It cannot be explained by temperature alone.
It shows that ions greatly accelerate the reaction.
Correct. It shows the synergy between ions and radicals.

etching-047.question: In plasma etching of high-aspect-ratio patterns, which phenomenon has electrons blocked by sidewalls so negative charge builds at the top of the pattern while positive ions are deflected at the bottom, causing profile defects and damage?
etching-047.explanation: Electrons move in random directions and seldom penetrate narrow features, so negative charge accumulates on upper sidewalls, while vertically accelerated ions reach and positively charge the bottom. This charge imbalance slows and deflects incoming ions, causing reduced bottom etch rates, notching, twisting and gate-dielectric damage. Pulsed plasmas that deliver negative ions or electrons to neutralize the charge are among the countermeasures.
choiceNotes: Correct. Electrons are shaded, creating a charge imbalance.
The tunnel effect is a quantum phenomenon of passing through a barrier.
The piezoelectric effect relates force and charge in piezoelectric materials.

etching-048.question: Which research-stage etching method neutralizes plasma-generated ions before they hit the wafer, suppressing charging and UV damage?
etching-048.explanation: Neutral-beam etching neutralizes plasma ions by passing them through a grid of narrow apertures, delivering directional neutral particles to the wafer. With no charge, there is no charging damage or deflection, and the grid blocks plasma UV, so almost no crystal defects result. It is promising for damage-sensitive work on compound semiconductors, 2D materials and ultra-fine GAA structures.
choiceNotes: Chemical mechanical polishing planarizes by polishing.
Correct. It processes with neutralized particles.
Wet etching uses solutions, not beams.

etching-049.question: Why are coatings such as yttrium oxide (Y2O3) used on the inner walls and parts of plasma etch tools?
choices: They resist plasma, especially fluorine-based plasma, and erode little, reducing particles and contamination
They make the tool look attractive
etching-049.explanation: Plasma erosion of chamber walls releases metal contamination such as aluminum and particles, and changing wall conditions shift the process. Yttrium oxide forms nonvolatile yttrium fluoride when attacked by fluorine, which stays on the surface, making it chemically stable and erosion-resistant in fluorine plasmas; it is used to coat walls and parts. Denser coating methods than thermal spraying are also being developed.
choiceNotes: Correct. They resist plasma and reduce particles and contamination.
Yttrium oxide is an insulating ceramic.
It is not for appearance.

etching-050.question: In plasma etch tools, what is the main role of the focus ring surrounding the wafer edge?
choices: To etch the back of the wafer
To shape the plasma and sheath near the wafer edge so that edge areas are etched with profiles and rates similar to the center
etching-050.explanation: Near the wafer edge, the electrode boundary bends the sheath (the ion-accelerating layer), so ions strike at an angle, tilting holes and changing etch rates. A silicon or quartz focus ring around the wafer makes the electrode appear to extend outward, keeping the sheath flat so chips within a few mm of the edge etch like those at the center. The ring erodes in the plasma, changing its effect, so its height is compensated or it is replaced periodically.
choiceNotes: It is not a part for etching the wafer back.
Correct. It makes edge processing match the center.
Wafer cooling is done with the electrostatic chuck and backside gas.
